mappings.note: Why the civilisation carries three names: one from the first excavated site (LO-109, archaeological evidence) and two from the rivers along which the first cities on the Indus grew (LO-113). Not LO-110, since no site has to be placed on a map.
A 200-word report on the civilisation's achievements requires pulling the whole chapter together (LO-115) around the first cities on the Indus (LO-113).
Planning a journey from Harappa to Kalibangan turns on knowing where the two sites lie relative to each other - locating important historical sites, which is LO-110.
What would astonish a Harappan in a modern kitchen: the answer rests on Harappan material life in the first cities. Not LO-109, since the item asks about their daily life, not about how we know it.
Lists ornaments, gestures and objects from the chapter's PICTURES that still look familiar - reading artefacts as evidence (LO-109) of Harappan life (LO-113).
What Dholavira's reservoir network shows about Harappan thinking - urban water management in the first cities, so LO-113. Not LO-110: the item is about the system, not where Dholavira is.
Seven hundred maintained brick wells at Mohenjo-daro and what they imply about civic planning - a feature of the first cities under LO-113.
Whether the Harappans had a high civic sense, argued from street layout, drains and public baths; still the urban character of the first cities.
Defines 'civilisation' as a complex, urban stage of society - the concept on which LO-113's first-cities development rests. Not LO-112, whose subject is early human cultures before cities.
Mesopotamia as one of the earliest civilisations; LO-113 explicitly asks pupils to relate developments in one place with another, which is what this comparison does.
Dates the mature phase to 2600-1900 BCE - the span of the first cities on the Indus. Not LO-115, since nothing is being synthesised, only recalled.
Why the Punjab and Sindh plains suited early agriculture: the farming base of the first cities (LO-113) on the Indus plains (LO-107).
Identifies the Sarasvati flowing through Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan and Gujarat - an Indian river (LO-107) that carried the civilisation's settlements (LO-113).
That the people are called Harappans after the first excavated city; a naming fact about the Indus civilisation, so LO-113.
Harappa as the first site systematically excavated in the 1920s - a fact about the archaeological work that produced the evidence, hence LO-109 rather than LO-110's map placement.
The 'First Urbanisation of India' names precisely the first-cities development that LO-113 covers.
Picks Dholavira in Gujarat from four sites, so the pupil must place it (LO-110) and know its water works (LO-113).
The Sarasvati praised in the Rig Veda's hymns - content of a literary work of the time, which LO-111 names. Not LO-107, because the question is about which text mentions it, not where the river ran.
Grid streets, standard bricks and planned quarters as the mark of Harappan cities - town planning in the first cities, so LO-113.
The two-part citadel-and-lower-town plan; another structural feature of the first cities, under the same outcome as the other planning items.
Standardised baked bricks as the building material - a hallmark of Harappan urbanism, hence LO-113.
Asks WHICH CITY held the Great Bath, so the site must be identified (LO-110) along with what such a structure says about the city (LO-113).

Rules out the general-public-bath reading BECAUSE most houses had their own bathrooms - an inference from excavated evidence (LO-109) about how the city worked (LO-113). Distinct from the item that merely asks where the Bath is.
Defines a fortification as the protective wall round Harappan cities; urban vocabulary of the first cities.
Defines a reservoir as a water store, the Dholavira feature; again the urban infrastructure of LO-113 rather than a site-location question.
A terracotta plough model from Banawali is an artefact (LO-109) that evidences Harappan tillage (LO-113). The model's value is entirely evidential, which is why LO-109 leads.
Turmeric, ginger and banana traces in cooking pots read as a varied diet - residue evidence (LO-109) about Harappan life (LO-113).
Carnelian as the favoured bead stone, sourced in Gujarat - a craft fact about the Harappans. Not LO-124, which is reserved here for their metalwork and other knowledge contributions.
Lothal's great brick basin, read as a dockyard: the site must be known (LO-110) and its point is maritime trade beyond India (LO-123).
What the thousands of seals were FOR - an interpretation drawn from an artefact class (LO-109) about how the cities did business (LO-113).
The one-horned 'unicorn' as the commonest seal motif; a description of the artefacts themselves, so LO-109 alone.
The Dancing Girl and the city she came from: site identification (LO-110) plus the bronze-casting skill that LO-124 covers under India's knowledge of metals.
A painted Lothal pot read as the thirsty-crow story - an interpretation of an artistic artefact, hence LO-109. Not LO-111, because the fable is not a literary work of the Harappan period.
Rejects widespread invasion among the causes of Harappan decline, keeping climate, the drying Sarasvati and falling yields - the end of the first-cities development under LO-113.
Matches each Harappan site to its modern state or region; purely locating important historical sites, so LO-110 alone.
Harappan trade reaching Mesopotamia, argued from seals and weights found abroad: contact with regions outside India (LO-123) evidenced by artefacts (LO-109).
Three achievements at once - drainage and town planning (LO-113) alongside bronze working (LO-124's knowledge of metals). The writing system has no outcome of its own, so it rides with LO-113.
Defines urbanism as the growth and planning of cities - the concept behind LO-113's first cities, and the counterpart of the 'civilisation' definition item.
Rakhigarhi placed in Haryana; a site-to-state item like the Dholavira pairing, so LO-110.
Rules out 'no trade' from the marks of an early civilisation, keeping government, cities and record-keeping - the general features of the first-cities development.
